A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HumorDB, with matching image pairs, three benchmark tasks, models and substantial shared results. All pages, including both versions' appendices, support comparison. Reporting inconsistencies are identifiable rather than evidence of missing material.

before.justification: v1 reports original human-rating studies, model evaluations on three tasks, original-image controls and qualitative attention and explanation analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds external-image controls, explanation evaluations, quantitative attention analyses, layerwise experiments and image-category results.

M1.justification: The prediction heads, feature-difference comparison procedure, losses and LoRA approach remain. v2 adds diagnostic procedures: attention/difference-map segmentation and applying the classifier to intermediate transformer layers (Sections 9–10). These extend the analysis methodology without establishing a redesigned humor-prediction model.

E1.justification: v2 adds an external negative-control scenario using 650 unedited, non-humorous images: 250 from MSCOCO and 400 from Places365. The core HumorDB tasks remain. Reporting separate scores for existing image categories does not establish that those categories were newly added.

E2.justification: The principal benchmark comparator set is retained. However, v2 Figure 7 introduces labels including AlexNetFL, CLIPLarge and DeiTLarge, while earlier labels such as ResNet150, ViT-Huge and ViTG-14 disappear from the corresponding original-image comparison. These labels conflict with v2's model list, leaving actual comparator substitutions versus labeling errors unresolved.

E3.justification: v2 introduces human explanation scoring on two 1–5 scales, synonym-based evaluation, quantitative attention metrics and layerwise testing. In-lab validation changes from 200 to 400 images, with at least five ratings per image newly specified. The main participant count changes from 550 to 650, although both appendices retain 850; actual recruitment changes remain unclear. The existing training grid and ten-epoch budget are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the earlier qualitative diagnostics with external editing-artifact controls, image-category breakdowns, quantitative human/automated explanation assessment, attention localization and layerwise probes. It also adds a prompt-sensitivity check, while omitting v1's brief dropout comparison. The original-image stress test already existed in v1 Appendix A.6.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 6 explicitly identifies binary-performance error bars as standard deviations; v1 Figure 5 did not identify their meaning. The five-run policy, with single runs for GPT-4o and Gemini-Flash, was already stated in v1 Appendix A.1 and remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive control, explanation, attention, layerwise and category results, including 81% external-control accuracy for ViT-G14. In-lab findings are replaced under the larger sample. Binary Figure 6a assigns approximately 78% to GPT-4 and 69% to word-fine-tuned LLaVA, versus approximately 70% and 78% respectively in v1 Figure 5a; this conflicts with the retained word-fine-tuning interpretation. The range table is unchanged, but the paired-only comparison results disappear. Table 1's reported total changes from 3,545 to 3,542 despite unchanged split rows.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs. The retained labeling and statistical criteria are unchanged; the added attention metrics and probing procedures constitute empirical methodology rather than new formal mathematical results.

C1.justification: The controlled visual-humor dataset and three-task benchmark remain the central contribution. v2 expands the abstract and introduction's contribution statements to include mechanistic interpretability and explanation evaluation, and foregrounds failures on sketches and humor localization.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning abstraction in sketches, learning beyond editing artifacts, depth-dependent humor processing and possible late-layer overfitting or feature collapse. It introduces substantive cultural and demographic limitations, including the predominantly young, US participant pool. v1's explicit discussion of offensive outputs and perpetuating stereotypes is removed.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies search-result caps, Photoshop/stable-diffusion editing, annotation counts, participant demographics, exact proprietary-model identifiers, explanation-scoring libraries and attention-processing thresholds. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to every underlying setting. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.7's explicit dataset license, Hugging Face/Croissant access information and maintenance statement disappear; the existing GitHub link remains.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges Chandrasekaran et al.'s earlier visual-humor dataset and positions HumorDB as extending prior datasets, qualifying v1's claimed lack of image-only datasets. It also adds DreamSim, MSCOCO and Places references and removes several broader humor/multimodal references. The main contrast with textual and audiovisual humor research remains.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, and the abstract, introduction, methods, results and discussion are substantially rewritten. Human-study procedures become structured lists, and the appendices are reorganized into supplementary Sections 7–13. The restructuring also introduces duplicated training-description paragraphs in Section 7.1.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. Multiple plots are redrawn with larger labels and revised axes or legends; reliability panels are separated, and the original-image analysis moves into the main text. Four tables and a layerwise figure are added, while the comparison figure loses its paired-only panel.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens validation and diagnosis through external controls, quantitative explanation/attention analyses, expanded in-lab validation and demographic limitations. However, new model-label and ranking inconsistencies in Figures 6–7 obscure central comparisons, while paired-only comparison results and explicit dataset-access documentation are lost. The substantial additions and reporting regressions leave the net quality direction unresolved from the PDFs alone.
